this is the mentor question for: https://www.pivotal-research.org/mentors#peter-hase:
Projects
Research Direction: Interpretability for monitoring and steering LLMs

CoT faithfulness methods. Can we make model CoT more monitorable by training models to faithfully report reward hacking behaviors in their CoT? See: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.20710

Goal introspection methods. Can we train models to report goals they have developed during earlier training steps (SL or RL)? See: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.05092

Interpretability for training. Can we use probes for truthfulness/honesty/faithfulness as reward models to steer model behavior? See: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.15515

Unsupervised elicitation. Can we elicit model \\u201cbeliefs\\u201d without supervision by training models to make consistent claims about the world? See: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2506.10139v1

What I'm looking for in a Mentee
You have the following technical background: familiarity with Python and Torch, have trained a deep learning model, have sampled from a language model locally (not just via API), and have done some scientific writing (e.g., a technical report or paper)

You do not need prior AI safety or interpretability research experience

You want to produce a research artifact (blog, paper, codebase) you can share with others

What I'm Like as a Mentor
In a normal week, I like to meet with my mentees once for a full hour to discuss research results, blockers, and plan out next steps. Outside of meetings, I try to be readily available over slack/email to answer questions as they arise. 

When spinning up or preparing a paper submission, I try to be available daily for feedback and input.

I try to encourage my mentees to be creative and independent. I want them to feel ownership of the research they do.

Bio         
Peter is a Postdoc at Stanford University and an AI Institute Fellow at Schmidt Sciences. His research focuses on LLM safety and interpretability. Previously, he has worked at Anthropic, Google, Meta, and the Allen Institute for AI.

Peter Hase

I am most interested in the Causes of introspection project. I have been conducting independent research into steering awareness on the model’s ability to detect steering vectors in it’s activations for which I’ve been using activation patching, direct logit attribution (DLA) to find the feature direction of introspection.\nConsistent with the MIA framework, current evidence suggests that internal representations of introspection lack robust linear separability. I propose exploring whether supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a diverse battery of introspective tasks can reinforce these underlying circuits. To ensure the resulting 'introspective' behavior is genuine rather than a superficial pattern-match, I will prioritize tasks with verifiable ground truths—such as refusal boundaries—to validate whether the model is truly accessing stable internal states.

I am most interested in the Causes of introspection project. I have been conducting independent research into steering awareness on the model’s ability to detect steering vectors in it’s activations for which I’ve been using activation patching, direct logit attribution (DLA) to find the feature direction of introspection.\nSince introspection isn't yet linearly separable in latent space, I want to test if targeted fine-tuning can 'boost' the existing circuits responsible for self-awareness. By selecting tasks with clear ground truths (e.g., refusal mechanisms), we can determine if this fine-tuning cultivates a stable, genuine introspective capability or just a localized heuristic. I see that introspection is not robustly linearly separable which is consistent with the Mechanisms of Introspective Awareness paper.

Focusing on the 'Causes of Introspection,' I have investigated 'steering awareness'—the model's capacity to detect steering vectors within it's own activations. Utilizing activation patching, direct logit attribution (DLA), and difference-in-means, I’ve found that while this awareness is behaviorally robust, it lacks linear separability, echoing the findings of Macar et al. I hypothesize that this mechanism serves as a foundational circuit for broader introspective tasks. To test this, I propose using SFT on tasks with verifiable ground truths (e.g., refusal detection) to observe performance transfer to held-out introspective tasks. Significant cross-task gains, alongside a control benchmark to rule out surface-level generalization, would suggest the existence of a genuine, shared introspective root.
